title: Daodejing, chapter 50 (Mawangdui silk manuscripts)
language: Classical Chinese (silk transcription; received text) / English
source: Mawangdui Laozi A and B silk manuscripts (plates of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng vol. 1, via Wikimedia Commons) + Wikisource column transcription + Wang Bi received text (Wikisource) + Legge 1891 English (Project Gutenberg)
description: Daodejing chapter 50 as written on the two Mawangdui silk manuscripts of the Laozi (before 168 BCE), with Legge's English and the received Chinese text.
introduction:
Chapter 50 of the Daodejing (Laozi), shown on the two oldest nearly complete copies of the work: the silk manuscripts Laozi A and Laozi B, found in 1973 in Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, Changsha (Hunan), a tomb sealed in 168 BCE. Laozi A is written in a script between seal and clerical forms and does not avoid the personal name of the Han founder Liu Bang (邦); it is commonly dated before 195 BCE. Laozi B is in clerical script, avoids 邦, and is commonly dated 194-180 BCE. Both put the De part (chapters 38-81) before the Dao part (chapters 1-37), and a few chapters stand in a different order from the received text.

Each section gives the silk transcription column by column, with the Jicheng column number before each column (for Laozi B, 上 and 下 are the upper and lower halves of a column, photographed on facing plates), and links to the plate that carries those columns. □ marks a lost character; ∠, ‧ and ﹦ are marks written on the silk (﹦ repeats the character before it). Below the transcription is the received text of the Wang Bi recension, which is the text James Legge translated in 1891; the silk wording differs from it, most visibly in 恆 for received 常 (the received text avoids the name of Emperor Wen, Liu Heng), in the frequent final particle 也, and in loan characters such as 胃 for 謂.
translator_notes: English: James Legge, The Tao Teh King (Sacred Books of the East 39, 1891); Legge's paragraph numbers are kept as superscripts.
Legge translated the received text, not the silk manuscripts. Where the silk wording differs, his English follows the received text shown under the transcription.
Silk transcription: Wikisource Page transcriptions of the Jicheng plates (revisions of 18 October 2026, marked not yet proofread on Wikisource), checked against the plates for each chapter opening.

translation.edition_text: 出生入死。生之徒，十有三；死之徒，十有三；人之生，動之死地，亦十有三。夫何故？以其生生之厚。蓋聞善攝生者，陸行不遇兕虎，入軍不被甲兵；兕無所投其角，虎無所措其爪，兵無所容其刃。夫何故？以其無死地。
translation.text:
1Men come forth and live; they enter (again) and die.

2Of every ten three are ministers of life (to themselves); and three are ministers of death.

3There are also three in every ten whose aim is to live, but whose movements tend to the land (or place) of death. And for what reason? Because of their excessive endeavours to perpetuate life.

4But I have heard that he who is skilful in managing the life entrusted to him for a time travels on the land without having to shun rhinoceros or tiger, and enters a host without having to avoid buff coat or sharp weapon. The rhinoceros finds no place in him into which to thrust its horn, nor the tiger a place in which to fix its claws, nor the weapon a place to admit its point. And for what reason? Because there is in him no place of death.
translation.scan_note: Laozi A (甲本), columns 24 to 27, on plate p. 96 of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng, vol. 1 (column numbers are printed under each plate; the columns run from right to left). Checked on the image: column 25 reads 徒十有三而民生﹦動皆之死地之十有三. The opening characters of this chapter are lost or not readable on this plate image, so these are the first characters that were confirmed. □ marks a character lost on the silk (16 in this section). Transcription and column numbers: Wikisource 老子 (帛書甲本), which follows the Jicheng column numbering. The English is Legge's translation of the received text, shown below the silk transcription; the silk wording differs from it in many places, so compare the two Chinese texts for the variants.
